videos.title: Gas Stoves and Kids' Asthma: What the 41-Study Analysis Found #Shorts
videos.description:
Do gas stoves affect children's breathing? Here's what the most-cited study found — and why scientists still debate it.

KEY POINTS
• Lin, Brunekreef & Gehring (Int J Epidemiol, 2013) pooled 41 studies on gas cooking, indoor nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), and asthma/wheeze in children.
• Gas cooking was associated with higher odds of childhood asthma (summary odds ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.18–1.48 — roughly 32% higher odds).
• Indoor NO₂ was associated with current wheeze (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.06–1.25). The association between a 15-ppb NO₂ increase and asthma was not statistically significant (OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.91–1.31).
• These are observational associations, not proof of cause and effect.
• A 2023 systematic review in Global Epidemiology (authors at Gradient; funded by the American Gas Association, per its disclosure) concluded that high heterogeneity and low study quality mean the literature does not provide sufficient evidence of a causal relationship.
• Practical steps either way (EPA): install and use an exhaust fan vented to the outdoors over gas stoves, and keep gas appliances properly adjusted.

SOURCES

videos.title: How Much Fresh Air Does Your House Need? The ASHRAE 62.2 Formula #Shorts
videos.description:
How much fresh air does a home actually need? Ventilation engineers use a simple formula.

KEY POINTS
• ASHRAE Standard 62.2 is the U.S. benchmark for residential ventilation.
• Whole-house rate (ASHRAE 62.2, I-P units): Qtot = 0.03 × floor area (ft²) + 7.5 × (bedrooms + 1) — i.e., 3 cfm per 100 ft² of floor plus 7.5 cfm per person, with occupancy counted as bedrooms + 1.
• Worked example (our calculation): 2,000 ft², 3 bedrooms → 60 cfm + 30 cfm = 90 cfm of continuous mechanical ventilation. Actual requirements depend on the edition of the standard, local code, and allowances such as infiltration credits.
• The U.S. Department of Energy notes that without proper ventilation, an otherwise insulated, airtight house can seal in pollutants and moisture; consider controlled ventilation after air sealing.
• System types include exhaust-only, supply-only, and balanced systems such as heat recovery (HRV) or energy recovery (ERV) ventilators. A qualified ventilation contractor can size a system to your home and local code.

• Wood smoke is a mix of gases and fine particles; EPA calls fine particles (PM2.5) the biggest health threat from smoke.

• Step 5: never burn trash, cardboard, plastics, painted/coated or pressure-treated wood, plywood, particleboard or anything with glue.
• Bonus: have your wood-burning appliance and chimney inspected annually, and keep smoke and CO alarms on every floor.

videos.description:
That number on your furnace filter has a specific meaning. Here's how MERV works, by the numbers.

• MERV (Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value) runs from 1 to 16 and reports a filter's ability to capture particles between 0.3 and 10 microns (ASHRAE Standard 52.2).

videos.title: Do Houseplants Clean Indoor Air? What 30 Years of Studies Show #Shorts
videos.description:
Can a few houseplants purify the air at home? A review of 30 years of chamber studies did the math.
